newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland talks chairman urges IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland talks chairman urges IRA truce.

text.p: The chairman of Northern Ireland peace talks, former U.S. senator George Mitchell, on Sunday added his voice to a chorus of appeals for a new IRA truce that would allow its Sinn Fein spokesmen to join the negotiations.
"Violence is not a path towards reconciliation or political stability in Northern Irleand. That has been demonstrated over the past 30 years or more," he told the BBC.

Mitchell was speaking the day after U.S. President Bill Clinton and British Prime Minister Tony Blair both urged the Irish Republican Army (IRA) to break with violence to allow its political wing Sinn Fein to claim a seat at the talks, which resume on Tuesday.

There was no immediate word from Sinn Fein, which shares the IRA goal of ending British rule of Northern Ireland, as to what its next step would be in a political climate soured by the IRA killing last Monday of two policemen in Lurgan.
But Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams said in a weekend statement that efforts to disarm the IRA as part of the talks remained an obstacle.
Mitchell, appointed last year to head the talks between pro-British Unionists and pro-Irish nationalists, said his own plan for breaking deadlock on the issue was the only route.
The former senator proposed last year that guerrilla groups negotiate disarmament in parallel with the talks, instead of before, as Britain originally insisted, or at the end.
"I think it is the only possibility," said Mitchell.

Blair is expected to spell out in detail his government's position on Sinn Fein's entry to the talks on Wednesday based on contacts his government officials had with chief Sinn Fein negotiator Martin McGuinness before the Lurgan killings.
Britain and its Irish partners in the peace process immediately broke off contacts with Sinn Fein after the double murders to express their revulsion.

Mitchell said the Belfast talks, which have been mired in what he called "painfully slow progress", should get down to substantive issues in September after the end of the province's flashpoint marching season by Protestant Loyalists.

The talks are supposed to cover Anglo-Irish proposals to ease tension between the two communities and the two parts of Ireland through a series of constitutional proposals and to increase economic cooperation to underpin peace.

The onset of the marching season has increased fears of a re-run of last year's province-wide violence, the worst for decades, when Protestants rioted to protest against the ban on a parade in the southern town of Portadown.
Police reinforcements were sent to Bellaghy, south of Londonderry, on Sunday to prevent trouble at a parade by the Orange Order which was rerouted after local Catholics objected.

Efforts to defuse tension received a boost when the Catholic Priest of a church at Harryville, near Ballymena, which has been picketed by Protestants every Saturday night for almost a year said he was calling off Saturday night services.
Northern Ireland police chief Ronnie Flanagan told the BBC it was "sincere gesture aimed at reducing tension".

Loyalists, so-called because of their allegiance to Britain, have protested outside the church in retaliation for the refusal of Catholic residents in the nearby village of Dubloy to allow a Protestant parade through a Catholic area.
